A faint mark or visible sign left by something which is lost, or has perished, or is no longer present.
d.x: the vestiges of ancient magnificence in Palmyra

d.g: A vestigial organ; a non-functional organ or body part that was once functional in an evolutionary ancestor.
The remaining portion of a partially suppressed sideband.

vestige.e: From French vestige, from Latin vestīgium (“footstep, footprint, track, the sole of the foot, a trace, mark”). Doublet of vestigium.

d.g: The hairs of plants, invertebrates and other non-mammalian organisms, taken as a whole.
Investiture (of a person with a specific role, powers etc.).

vestiture.e: From Medieval Latin vestitura, from Latin vestire.

d.g: A robe, gown, or other article of clothing worn as an indication of office.

d.g: Any of the special articles of clothing worn by members of the clergy etc., especially a garment worn at the celebration of the Eucharist.

vestment.e: From Middle English vestement, vestment, from Old French vestement, from Latin vestīmentum. By surface analysis, vest + -ment. Compare French vêtement.

A room in a church where the clergy put on their vestments and where these are stored; also used for meetings and classes.
d.x: The choirboys change into their cassocks in the vestry.

d.g: An assembly of persons (ad hoc or recurrent) who manage parochial affairs; so called because usually held in a vestry.
A committee of parishioners elected to administer the temporal affairs of a parish.
d.x: Near-synonyms: parochial church council, PCC, parish council (ecclesiastical sense, uncommon)

vestry.e: From Anglo-Norman vesterie, from Old French vestiaire (“room for vestments, dressing room”), from Latin vestiarium (“wardrobe”). Doublet of vestiary.

d.g: A member of a parochial vestry, especially one who is a man.

A covering of, or like, clothing.

vesture.e: From Middle English vesture (noun) and vesturen (verb), from Anglo-Norman, from Old French vesteüre, from Vulgar Latin vestītūra (“clothing”), from Latin vestītus, perfect passive participle of vestiō (“to clothe”), from vestis (“garment”).

d.g: a green or yellow or brown mineral consisting of a hydrated silicate;  it occurs as crystals in limestone and is used a gemstone
A yellow, green or brown mineral, a mixed calcium, magnesium and aluminium silicate sometimes used as a gemstone.

vesuvianite.e: English Vesuvian Proto-Indo-European *-tósder. Ancient Greek -της (-tēs)der. Ancient Greek -ῑ́της (-ī́tēs)der. Latin -ītēsbor. French -iteder. English -ite English vesuvianite From Vesuvian + -ite.

d.g: To thoroughly check or investigate particularly with regard to providing formal approval.

d.g: Any of several leguminous plants, of the genus Vicia, often grown as green manure and for their edible seeds.

vetch.e: From Middle English vecche, fecche, ficche, from Old Northern French veche, variant of Old French vece, from Latin vicia. Doublet of fitch.

any other member of genus Lathyrus.

vetchling.e: From vetch (“leguminous plant of genus Vicia”) + -ling.

veterinarian.e: From Latin veterīnārius (“cattle doctor”) + -an, from veterīnae (“beasts of burden, draught-”), probably from vehō (“to convey, draw”), or from vetus (“old”). By surface analysis, veterinary + -an.

An invocation of that right.

d.g: An authoritative prohibition or negative; a forbidding; an interdiction.

The state of being vexed, annoyed, or irritated; annoyance, irritation; also, disappointment, discontentment, unhappiness; (countable) an instance of this.
d.x: "Indeed you perplex me intolerably;" cried Cecilia, vvith ſome vexation, "VVhy, Sir, vvill you not be more explicit?"

To shift aft.

veer.e: Middle Dutch vierenbor. English veer Borrowed from Middle Dutch vieren (“to slacken”).

d.g: To grow or sprout.
To spread abnormally.
To live or spend a period of time in a dull, inactive, unchallenging way.

vegetate.e: Borrowed from Latin vegetātus, perfect passive participle of vegetō (“to enliven, to arouse”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

d.g: To touch (a body part) lightly so as to excite the surface nerves and cause uneasiness, laughter, or spasmodic movements.
To twitch or move convulsively.
To tickle, provoking twitching and laughter.
To criticize in a somewhat irritating way; to carp at.

vellicate.e: From Latin vellicatus, past participle of vellicare (“to twitch”). Cognate with Spanish pellizcar (“to pinch”).

d.g: To treat with great respect and deference.
To revere or hold in awe.

venerate.e: First attested in 1623; borrowed from Latin venerātus, perfect active participle of veneror (“to worship, venerate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

d.g: To carry out a venesection

ventilate.e: From Middle English, borrowed from Latin ventilātus, past participle of ventilō.

verbalise.e: Partly from Middle French verbaliser and partly from verbal + -ise.

verbalize.e: Partly from Middle French verbaliser and partly from verbal + -ize.

To derive a verb from a pre-existing noun.

to turn (prose) into poetry; rewrite in verse form

versify.e: From Middle English versifien, from Old French versifier, learned borrowing from Latin versificāre (“versify”), from versus (see verse) + faciō (“make”).

Vesicular.
